items.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998
items.q: I worked for Dave Grusin a lot... Tom Scott and some of those people.

ctx.x: Well you said a couple of minutes ago you were talking about the studio music and you said most of it was just craft. And at first I thought you were going to say crap. But I think it’s a telling thing that you didn’t say that, because even playing on a Rice-a-Roni commercial, you have to do what’s required, and not more. Because I’ve heard plenty of players who can play the piano like crazy but they don’t understand the gig — if it’s solo piano if it’s in a restaurant or something.

Yeah. And that’s where the professional, again, yeah you’re absolutely right. There’s craft and there’s art as far as I’m concerned. It’s kind of like the old line, years ago someone said, “There’s music and there’s the music business.” And they’re very often two very different things. Yeah. On any given day in a Hollywood studio, and it would be the same in New York, I was sitting with the greatest players in the world, guys who © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

could sit in a symphony orchestra, who could do all kinds of stuff. So there was nothing demeaning or ridiculous about being there, I mean you were lucky to be there. But a lot of times the product you were going for was maybe — this, we’re not talking here Pierre Boulez, but on the other hand, in many cases it was wonderful music, great writers who took it very seriously, even if it was just fairly innocuous film, took the writing very seriously. I worked for Dave Grusin a lot. Dave Grusin wrote beautiful stuff…
